introduction-the-most-critical-engineeri.core: Hiring decides the team's future capability more than any single technical decision. A bad hire costs months, and a great one multiplies output for years, so hiring deserves engineering rigour: structure, calibration and bias reduction.

first_principles.problem: Engineers see interviewing as a distraction, run ad-hoc interviews and make inconsistent decisions.
truths: Bad hires are costly to undo.

analogy.title: A sports team's recruitment
analogy.story: The coach's most important job is choosing the squad, not calling plays.
analogy.breaks: Over-rigid processes miss unconventional talent, so balance structure with judgement.

example.title: The cost of a bad hire
flow: Recruiting + onboarding: ~3 months of team time
example.outcome: hiring treated as a core engineering activity.

check.q: Why should hiring get engineering rigour?
check.a: It shapes long-term team capability, and bad hires are very expensive to undo.

designing-the-loop-structure-vs-gut-feel.core: Structured interviews (pre-defined competencies, consistent questions, scoring rubrics, specific evidence) predict job performance far better than unstructured chats, and they reduce bias.

first_principles.problem: Interviewers ask whatever they like and decide on 'gut feel', which favours candidates like themselves.
derivation: Define **competencies** per role (coding, system design, collaboration).
Use **standard questions + rubrics** (what strong, mixed and weak look like).

analogy.title: Judging a cooking competition
analogy.story: Judges use the same criteria (taste, presentation, technique) for every dish, not 'I liked it'.
analogy.breaks: Rubrics can become rigid. Allow follow-up questions within a competency.

check.q: Why are structured interviews better than unstructured ones?
check.a: They're more predictive of job performance and reduce bias through consistent questions and evidence-based scoring.

the-bar-raiser-the-guardian-of-quality.core: A bar raiser (Amazon's model) is a trained interviewer from outside the hiring team, who has veto power and the mandate to ensure each hire raises the average, which protects against desperation hires.

first_principles.problem: An understaffed team lowers its standards to fill seats quickly, and the long-term quality of the team erodes.
derivation: Put them **outside** the hiring team (no urgency bias).
Ask: is this candidate **better than half the current team at this level**?

analogy.title: An independent building inspector
analogy.story: The builder wants to finish fast; the inspector ensures the structure meets the code anyway.
analogy.breaks: Veto power used arbitrarily causes friction, so bar raisers need calibration too.

example.title: A desperate team's candidate
flow: Bar raiser: no hire, the bar would drop
example.outcome: a hiring bar that rises over time.

check.q: Why is the bar raiser from outside the hiring team?
check.a: To avoid the urgency bias that pressures the hiring team to lower standards.

the-debrief-voting-in-the-dark.core: Debriefs are where bias spreads: the most senior or first speaker anchors everyone. Have interviewers submit written feedback and a vote independently before the meeting (voting in the dark), then discuss the evidence.

first_principles.problem: The hiring manager says 'I loved them' first, and everyone else quietly adjusts their opinion.
truths: Anchoring and conformity bias group decisions.
Independent judgements are more accurate in aggregate.
Written evidence keeps the discussion grounded.
derivation: Interviewers **write feedback + vote before** seeing others'.
The **decision maker** (often the bar raiser) facilitates and decides.

analogy.title: A sealed-bid auction
analogy.story: Bids submitted secretly reflect real valuations; open bidding creates herd behaviour.
analogy.breaks: Rigid process can suppress useful discussion, so the goal is to reduce anchoring, not to stop debate.

example.title: Independent votes reveal a split
flow: Votes: Hire, Hire, No-hire (design), Strong hire
Decision: no hire at senior; offer at mid-level

check.q: What does 'voting in the dark' prevent?
check.a: Anchoring and conformity bias, where early or senior opinions sway everyone else.

calibration-what-does-senior-actually-me.core: Without calibration, 'Senior' means different things on different teams. Calibration aligns interviewers and leveling decisions to a shared ladder through examples, shadowing, periodic reviews of decisions and level-specific rubrics.

first_principles.problem: One team's 'senior' would be mid-level elsewhere, which causes unfairness, pay inconsistency and mobility problems.
derivation: Use **level-specific rubrics** tied to the career ladder.
Interviewers **shadow and reverse-shadow** before interviewing alone.
Run **hiring committees** for consistency across teams.

analogy.title: Calibrating scales in different shops
analogy.story: Every shop's '1 kg' must weigh the same, or customers are cheated.
analogy.breaks: Too much central control slows hiring, so balance consistency with speed.

example.title: A quarterly calibration session
example.outcome: titles that mean the same everywhere.

check.a: It keeps titles, expectations and pay consistent across teams, which supports fairness and mobility.
